title: Serum Sodium Correction Trend
scenario: A 60-year-old client admitted with symptomatic hyponatremia is started on a hypertonic saline infusion. The nurse reviews serial serum sodium values drawn every four hours.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical
questions.stem: Reviewing the flowsheet, how does the nurse best interpret the rate of sodium correction over the first 12 hours?

options.text: The correction is appropriately gradual at about 11 mEq/L over 12 hours
The correction is dangerously slow and the infusion should be doubled
The correction is complete because sodium is now within normal range
The correction is too rapid and risks fluid volume overload

questions.rationale: Sodium rose from 116 to 127 mEq/L over 12 hours, roughly 11 mEq/L, which stays within the safe limit of about 8-10 mEq/L per 24 hours and avoids osmotic demyelination. The value is still below normal, so correction is not complete.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical
questions.stem: Based on the trend, which nursing actions are appropriate at this time? Select all that apply.

options.text: Continue to monitor serum sodium every 4 hours
Watch for new dysarthria, dysphagia, or altered consciousness
Notify the provider if sodium rises more than 10-12 mEq/L in 24 hours
Administer a rapid bolus of hypertonic saline to speed correction
Stop all sodium monitoring now that the client is oriented

questions.rationale: Safe management of hyponatremia correction requires ongoing sodium monitoring, serial neuro checks for signs of osmotic demyelination, and provider notification if correction exceeds safe limits. Rapidly bolusing hypertonic saline or stopping monitoring would endanger the client.
